summary: Describes how to use the ATM call-setup procedures from UNI Signalling 4.0 efficiently to support IP over ATM networks. It is on the standards track and builds on earlier IP over ATM work.

plainLanguage.summary: ATM is a network technology where each connection is set up with its own signalling messages before data flows. This document says what an IP router should put in those messages: which fields are required, which values to use for the IP packet size and the encapsulation, and how to ask for the service the site has actually bought.

subtitle: How IP endpoints ask an ATM network for the service they need, using UNI Signalling 4.0.

tldr.problem: The ATM Forum's fourth version of its user-network signalling specification added features that IP over ATM could use, but no document said which information elements an IP endpoint should put in its setup messages or how to choose between them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the information elements a SETUP message must and may contain for IP, gives the values for the adaptation layer and low layer information elements, and explains the traffic management choices, including traffic parameter negotiation and the tagging option.
tldr.outcome: IP endpoints get a defined way to request ATM service in sites with switched virtual circuits, following RFC 1755, which this document updates on virtual circuit teardown. It covers best-effort IP only.

sections.title: What This Document Adds
sections.content:
The memo describes how to efficiently use the ATM call control signalling procedures defined in UNI Signalling 4.0 to support IP over ATM environments as described in RFC 2225 and in RFC 2332. Among the new features found in UNI Signalling 4.0 are Available Bit Rate signalling and traffic parameter negotiation. The memo highlights the features of UNI Signalling 4.0 that provide IP entities with capabilities for requesting ATM service in sites with SVC support, whether it is private ATM or publicly provisioned ATM, in which case the SVC support is probably configured inside PVPs.

The document is only relevant to IP when used as the well known best effort connectionless service. In particular, it does not pertain to IP in the presence of implemented IP Integrated Services: the topic of IP with Integrated Services over ATM is to be handled by a different specification, or set of specifications, being worked on in the ISSLL working group.

This specification is a follow-on to RFC 1755, which is based on UNI 3.1 signalling, and readers are assumed to be familiar with RFC 1755.
sections.plainLanguage: The scope is narrow on purpose: plain best-effort IP. Where the network guarantees quality per flow, the signalling needs a different treatment, and the document says so rather than guessing.

sections.title: The Signalling 4.0 Features That Matter
sections.content:
UNI Signalling version 4.0 is the ATM Forum follow-on specification to UNI 3.1 signalling. Among the new features in SIG 4.0, those of particular interest to IP over ATM environments are:

  • Available Bit Rate (ABR) signalling for point-to-point calls
  • Traffic parameter negotiation
  • Frame discard support
  • Leaf Initiated Join capability
  • ATM Anycast capability
  • Switched Virtual Path service

The memo highlights the first three capabilities listed above. The last three are not discussed because models for their use in IP over ATM environments have not yet been defined: the ION working group is considering the applicability of Leaf Initiated Join and Group Addressing to the RFC 2022 problem space, and Anycast addressing is being explored as a technique for supporting server discovery in ATM networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Of the six things UNI 4.0 added, the document covers three: a rate-based service, the ability to negotiate traffic parameters, and a way to discard whole damaged frames. The other three were left out because nobody had worked out how IP would use them.

sections.title: When a Virtual Circuit Should Come Down
sections.content:
Section 3 in RFC 1755 introduces requirements of virtual circuit management intended to prevent VC thrashing, excessive VC consumption and other related problems. This section updates the requirements of RFC 1755 related to VC teardown.

In environments running layer 3 signalling protocols, such as RSVP, over ATM, data VCs might correspond to layer 3 reserved flows, even if the VC is a best effort VC. In such environments it is beneficial for VCs to be torn down only when the layer 3 reservation has expired. In other words, it is more efficient for the sender of a layer 3 reserved flow to initiate VC tear-down when the receiver has ceased refreshing the reservation. To support such behaviour, systems implementing a Public ATM UNI interface and serving as the called party of a VCC MUST NOT use an inactivity timer on such a VCC by default. A system MAY use an inactivity timer on such a VCC if configured to do so.
sections.plainLanguage: If a flow has a reservation above ATM, the ATM circuit should stay up as long as the reservation does. So the network side, which is the called party, must not quietly tear the circuit down on a timer unless an operator has explicitly asked for that.

sections.title: What a SETUP Message Must Contain
sections.content:
Signalling messages are structured to contain mandatory and optional variable length information elements. A SETUP message which establishes an ATM connection to be used for IP and multiprotocol interconnection calls MUST contain the following information elements: AAL Parameters, ATM Traffic Descriptor, Broadband Bearer Capability, Broadband Low Layer Information, QoS Parameter, Called Party Number and Calling Party Number.

It MAY, under certain circumstances, contain the following: Calling Party Subaddress, Called Party Subaddress, Transit Network Selection, and, new in SIG 4.0, Minimum Acceptable ATM Traffic Descriptor, Alternative ATM Traffic Descriptor, ABR Setup Parameters, ABR Additional Parameters, Connection Scope Selection, Extended QoS Parameters and End-to-End Transit Delay.

In SIG 4.0, like UNI 3.1, the AAL Parameters and the Broadband Low Layer Information elements are optional in a SETUP message. However, in support of IP over ATM these two MUST be included. The appendix of the document shows a sample setup message.
sections.plainLanguage: A call setup for IP has a fixed list of fields that must be filled in, and a longer list that may be filled in. Two of the fields that are optional for a general ATM call are required here, because they are what tells the network to carry IP.

sections.title: The Adaptation Layer and the Encapsulation
sections.content:
The AAL Parameters element carries information about the ATM adaptation layer to be used on the connection, and the parameters specified in it are the same as those specified in the ATM Forum's Public Private Network Interface specification. The element carries an AAL type of 5, forward and backward maximum SDU sizes of 65,535 octets, described as the desired IP MTU, and an SSCS type of 0, meaning a null SSCS.

This shows maximum size MTUs. In practice, most sites have used 9,180 octet IP MTUs for ATM.

Selection of an encapsulation to support IP over an ATM virtual circuit is done using the Broadband Low Layer Information element, along with the AAL Parameters element and the B-LLI negotiation procedure. The B-LLI negotiation is described in Appendix D of the ATM Forum specification, and the procedures remain the same for this SIG 4.0 based specification. The element as used for LLC/SNAP encapsulation carries a layer 2 identifier of 2 and a user information layer of 12, meaning lan_llc, which is ISO 8802/2.
sections.plainLanguage: Two fields decide how IP rides over ATM: the adaptation layer type, which is AAL 5, and the lower-layer encapsulation, which is LLC/SNAP. The maximum packet size field allows a very large value, but in practice sites settled on 9,180 octets.

sections.title: Which ATM Service to Ask For
sections.content:
The ATM Forum Traffic Management sub-working group has completed version 4.0 of their specification, which focuses primarily on the definition of the ABR service category. As opposed to the Unspecified Bit Rate traffic class, ABR uses a rate-based flow control mechanism to assure certain traffic guarantees, bandwidth and delay. There has been much debate on whether IP benefits from ABR, and if so how IP should use it. The IP Integrated Services and RSVP models in IP add complexity, because mapping IP traffic classes to ATM traffic classes is not straightforward.

The document attempts only to present the required IP to ATM signalling interface for IP over ATM systems that do not support Integrated Services yet. It is an attempt to cause IP over ATM vendors to support enough options for signalling the traffic characteristics of virtual circuits serving non-IIS IP datagrams, and it aims to give guidance to ATM system administrators so that they can configure their IP over ATM entities to conform to the varied services that their ATM provider may have sold to them.

An IP over ATM interface may be configured to support all the defined ATM Service Categories: CBR, CBR with CLR specified, which is loss-permitting CBR, ABR, UBR, real time VBR and non-real time VBR. The ATM Traffic Descriptor, Broadband Bearer Capability and QoS Parameter elements together define the signalling view of ATM traffic management. The Extended QoS parameters and the End-to-End Transit Delay elements may be used to provide more specifics about traffic requirements, though the document gives no explicit recommendations on their use.

Annex 9 of the UNI 4.0 specification describes a set of allowable combinations of traffic and QoS related parameters. This set includes all forms of non-IIS IP signalling configurations that MUST be implemented in ATM endsystems to accommodate varied sites' needs. The principle is that IP over ATM service may be available in different sites by different types of procured ATM service: for one site a CBR virtual path might be cost-effective, and then the switched circuits that IP over ATM without Integrated Services must establish must be CBR. Similarly, VBR or ABR virtual paths could be provisioned. The intent of the document is to specify the use of the most sensible parameters within this non-IIS configuration: for instance, for non-IIS VBR the sustainable cell rate value may need to be hand-configured for IP users, or for ABR the peak cell rate value may be the link rate with a zero minimum cell rate.

Ideally the document could recommend specific values for the various table parameters that would offer the most sensible IP over ATM service. Nevertheless, it is not possible to mandate specific values given the varied scenarios of procured ATM service. The tables of Annex 9 are replicated in the appendix of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Six ATM service categories are available, and the right one depends on what the site has bought. A site with a constant-bit-rate virtual path can only have constant-bit-rate circuits, so the IP endpoint has to ask for that. The document says to configure for the service in hand rather than assume one best setting.

sections.title: Negotiating Parameters, Tagging and Frame Discard
sections.content:
SIG 4.0 allows certain traffic parameters to be negotiated during the call establishment phase; traffic parameters cannot be renegotiated after the call is active. Two new elements make negotiation possible: the Minimum Acceptable ATM Traffic Descriptor element allows negotiation of PCR parameters, and the Alternative ATM Traffic Descriptor element allows negotiation of other traffic parameters. A SETUP or CONNECT message may include only one of the two, so the calling party may offer either an alternative or a minimum, not both. IP over ATM entities SHOULD take advantage of this capability whenever possible, and to do so SHOULD specify PCR equal to the link rate in the ATM Traffic Descriptor element of the SETUP message and a minimum of zero PCR in the Minimum Acceptable ATM Traffic Descriptor element.

The Traffic Descriptor element contains a tagging subfield used for indicating whether the network is allowed to tag the source's data cells. Tagging in the network may occur during periods of congestion or when the source's traffic has violated the traffic contract for the connection. SIG 4.0 and Traffic Management 4.0 define two modes of UBR: UBR.1, which disables tagging, and UBR.2, which enables tagging. In some network environments there is no potential for UBR traffic sources to violate the connection traffic contract, because either the user's terminal equipment supports traffic shaping or the network does not enforce the peak cell rate. In such environments the user SHOULD specify no tagging in the SETUP message, that is UBR.1. Specifying no tagging indicates to the network that cells should be dropped during periods of congestion instead of being randomly marked as low priority, so that cells of packets that the source itself has marked as low priority are dropped first, preserving the source's characterization of the traffic.

On the other hand, when the network applies the peak cell rate to the Usage Parameter Control function, meaning it enforces it, and traffic shaping is not enabled at the source, the source has the potential to violate the traffic contract and SHOULD therefore signal for tagging, that is UBR.2. Tagging allows the source's non-conforming cells to be tagged and forwarded instead of dropped.

The frame discard capability in SIG 4.0 is primarily based on the Partial and Early Packet Discard strategy. Its use is defined for any of the ATM services except loss-less CBR. Frame discard signalling MUST be supported by all IP over ATM entities, and it is RECOMMENDED that frame discard be signalled for all IP switched virtual circuits, because it has been proven to increase throughput under network congestion. Signalling for frame discard is done by setting the frame discard bit in the Traffic Management Options subfield in the Traffic Descriptor element. It is possible that not all network entities in the path support frame discard, but it is required that they all forward the signalling.
sections.plainLanguage: Three choices are described here. Ask for a peak rate of the whole link and settle for anything, so the network can pick. Decide whether the network may mark your cells as low priority or must drop them, based on whether the network polices your traffic. And ask for whole frames to be discarded when they are damaged, which avoids reassembling frames that can never be completed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The ATM Forum Security sub-working group is currently defining security mechanisms in ATM. The group has yet to produce a specification, so it is premature to begin defining IP over ATM signalling's use of ATM security. The ATM Forum is working on authentication mechanisms for signalling and on mechanisms for providing data integrity and confidentiality, for example encryption. The lack of these ATM security mechanisms prevents the authentication of the originator of signalling messages, such as a connection setup request or a connection teardown request.

IP Security can be applied to IP datagrams over ATM virtual circuits to overcome the lack of security at the ATM layer.
sections.plainLanguage: There was no ATM security mechanism to rely on, so the signalling messages themselves cannot be attributed to anyone. The document points instead at IP-level security, applied to the IP packets carried over the circuit.

items.label: constant bit rate
items.desc: A fixed amount of bandwidth for the life of the call.

items.label: loss-permitting CBR
items.desc: Constant bit rate where some loss is allowed.

items.label: available bit rate
items.desc: Rate-based flow control that assures bandwidth and delay guarantees.

items.label: unspecified bit rate
items.desc: The best effort class, which enforces no bandwidth commitment.

viz.caption: AN EXCERPT FROM THE SAMPLE SETUP MESSAGE (RFC 2331 APPENDIX A)

data.title: Sample SETUP message
data.code:
aal_parameters
   aal_type                         5        (AAL 5)
   fwd_max_sdu_size               (xmit IP MTU value)
   bkw_max_sdu_size      (recv IP MTU, 0 for disallowing return traffic)
   sscs_type                        0        (null SSCS)

traffic_descriptor
   fwd_peak_cell_rate_0_1         (link rate)
   bkw_peak_cell_rate_0_1         (link rate)
   fwd_frame_discard                1   (on)
   bkw_frame_discard                1   (on if return traffic indicated)
   tagging_bkw                      1   (on)
   tagging_fwd                      1   (on if return traffic indicated)
   best_effort_indication         190   (on)

minimum_acceptable_traffic_descriptor
   fwd_peak_cell_rate_0_1           0
   bkw_peak_cell_rate_0_1           0

bb_bearer_capability     /* a coding for specifying UBR like service */
   bearer_class                    16      (BCOC-X)
   atm_transfer_capability         10      (nrt-vbr)
   susceptibility_to_clipping       0      (not susceptible to clipping)
   user_plane_configuration         0      (point_to_point)

bb_low_layer_information
   layer_2_id                       2
   user_information_layer          12       (lan_llc - ISO 8802/2)

qos_parameter
   qos_class_fwd                    0        (class 0)
   qos_class_bkw                    0        (class 0)
